paragraphs: When I realized what 6.1 Sol Max costs on the $500 subscription, I went back to a dream task while I still could: go through my entire product for every possible bug, mismatch, stale piece of code and duplicate.
I've tried this with every new model release (apart from Astra; that was too expensive). Every time, I've found that no model could properly study a codebase this size.

I used to think that when I asked PRO to find bugs and got a list back, it had really examined everything. That was never true. PRO, like every other model, just looked at the GitHub repo, opened a selection of files, no more than a couple dozen, and packaged what it found as if to say, 'I've found it all.'
That still had value: it found things we could fix. But it missed nearly everything buried in the files, so a proper refactor of the project remained out of reach.

For the first time, 6.1 Sol Max approached my request differently. It spent an hour and a half turning the repo over, then proposed a tracking system that would have fresh sessions move from file to file, map the codebase and record bugs, duplicates, code needing refactoring and points of failure.
We also agreed that after more than forty compactions, a session would finish its current finding and hand the ledger over to a new session to continue.

Honestly, I didn't expect it to work this time either, but I tried. The process has now run for about 36 hours, passed the baton to its fourth session, and scanned 1,003 of the repo's 3,870 files in detail.
No wonder earlier models never managed a proper review. They were less capable and finished in a couple of hours; they probably saw a random sliver of the project and stopped there.

When I read through the 78 findings, I was pleasantly surprised. Almost none looked fabricated or dubious. Now I can discuss each one with PRO: when it arose, what came before it, why it happened and how to fix it reliably for this project.
While it's cheap, I'd recommend that anyone with a huge repo try something similar. Later it might cost tens of thousands of dollars in tokens again, and the appetite for it will disappear =)

The auditor running on Sol 6.1 Max has only just finished. It worked continuously since the model was released and used three subagents to speed things up; without them, I reckon it would have taken at least fifteen days.
This is one of those rare tasks where subagents can help rather than get in the way.
It went through 3,900 files and found 220 problems across 62 categories.

Most are nasty, real bugs of the kind where the expected behavior would fail under particular conditions. Some aren't fatal, but many would simply break a feature and cost me hours just to understand what happened, never mind the unhappy client who thinks they've signed up for a pile of shit.

The difficult part turned out to be coordinating the fixes. I let it run ten sessions at once, but even with three subagents helping review the fixers' work, the queue kept growing. In two days I barely got twenty fixes through, while 28 worktrees waited more than ten hours each to be reviewed.
That's where Dot helped.

I described the bottleneck and asked Dot to design a way to distribute tasks and review them without building up a queue. Overnight, Dot got the fixes moving at a steady pace of roughly two fully tested and deployed fixes an hour, with twenty sessions working at any given moment.
At that load, about 30% of the weekly limit on the $500 subscription went in the past ten hours. There's one reset left, so I think the whole job will be done by Wednesday :)
Dot also tested different reasoning levels for Sol 6.1 and concluded it was better to keep every session on Max.
Last night, a few drinks and the fourteen hours of Claude I had left before the reset gave me the idea to make a new game based on Arcomage.
The brainstorm with Fable went well, and by around three in the morning we had a plan. I still had about 87% of the weekly limit unused. I put the plan into a goal and went to sleep.
In the morning I looked: only 3% of the weekly limit was left. Fuck, it got through it)))
I haven't looked at the result yet. I'm off to walk the dog; please take a look (it should appear as a new game in the arena).
I'm really curious what it managed to make))))

What stands out is that, to balance the game, it took my request literally: 'even if it takes hundreds of millions of games, just make the balance tight, fuck.' It ran 3.5 BILLION simulated games to try to reach that balance :)
It worked for more than ten hours, bringing in Opus 5 sessions for side tasks and Codex for the artwork. I respect that)
